---
title: "Random effects and partial pooling"
---

The [preceding page](fixed-and-random-effects.qmd) separated planned population contrasts from variation across sampled groups. A random-effects model represents the latter through a shared group distribution and partial pooling.

Suppose three speakers have observed mean acoustic durations of vowel tokens of 90, 110, and 160 ms. The first two means are based on 20 tokens each. The third is based on only 2 tokens. Treating 160 ms as an equally stable speaker estimate ignores the difference in information. These token measurements describe duration; they do not by themselves establish a phonological length category.

A random effects model addresses this problem through [**partial pooling**](https://bruno.nicenboim.me/bayescogsci/ch-hierarchical.html). Each speaker has a distinct deviation, but those deviations belong to one estimated population distribution.

## Model deviations from a shared center

Let $\beta_0$ be the population baseline. Give speaker $j$ a deviation $b_j$:

$$
\text{speaker baseline}_j
=\beta_0+b_j.
$$

Model the deviations as draws from a common distribution:

$$
b_j\sim\mathcal{N}(0,\tau^2).
$$

The parameter $\tau$ is the standard deviation of speaker baselines around the population baseline. The deviation $b_j$ is the random effect introduced on the [preceding page](fixed-and-random-effects.qmd).

The zero center is not a claim that speakers do not differ. It defines $\beta_0$ as the population center and lets positive and negative deviations occur around it. The parameter $\tau$ measures the extent of those differences.

## Comparing three pooling strategies

[**Complete pooling**](https://bruno.nicenboim.me/bayescogsci/ch-hierarchical.html) ignores persistent speaker differences. Every speaker receives the same baseline $\beta_0$.

[**No pooling**](https://bruno.nicenboim.me/bayescogsci/ch-hierarchical.html) estimates an unrelated baseline for every speaker. The two token speaker estimate relies only on two observations.

[**Partial pooling**](https://bruno.nicenboim.me/bayescogsci/ch-hierarchical.html) combines each speaker's observations with the estimated population distribution. Speakers can differ, but the amount of evidence for each difference matters.

These strategies represent different claims. Complete pooling says the group labels add no persistent structure. No pooling says the observed groups share no informative population relation. Partial pooling says the groups vary and that their deviations arise from a common population.

## Examining where shrinkage comes from

In a simple random-intercept model with known variances, the estimated speaker deviation has the form

$$
\widehat b_j
=w_j(\overline y_j-\beta_0),
$$

where

$$
w_j
=\frac{n_j\tau^2}
{\sigma^2+n_j\tau^2}.
$$

The quantity $w_j$ is between zero and one. It determines how much of the raw speaker difference is retained.

If $n_j$ is small or the residual variance $\sigma^2$ is large, $w_j$ is closer to zero. The estimate moves toward the population baseline. If $n_j$ is large and the observations are consistent, $w_j$ is closer to one. The estimate remains closer to the speaker's raw mean.

This movement is called [**shrinkage**](https://bruno.nicenboim.me/bayescogsci/ch-hierarchical.html) or partial pooling. It is a consequence of the joint probability model, not a correction applied after unrelated speaker means have been estimated.

## Keeping two variances separate

The group standard deviation

$$
\tau
$$

describes stable between speaker baseline variation. The residual standard deviation

$$
\sigma
$$

describes token variation around a speaker's baseline and the modeled predictor effects.

One cannot substitute for the other. A large residual variance does not represent persistent speaker differences. A large group variance does not represent token noise within a speaker.

## Understanding the exchangeability claim

The shared distribution treats speaker labels as exchangeable after conditioning on included predictors. Before observing the responses, swapping labels p01 and p02 does not change the model. The labels identify groups, but the model does not give one label a special distribution without a predictor that justifies it.

If speakers differ systematically by measured age or dialect, that structure should enter the population relation. The random effects then describe remaining speaker variation after those predictors are known.

Exchangeability is thus conditional rather than absolute. It asks whether the unexplained deviations can reasonably share one distribution. A model that pools speakers across known populations with very different variance structures may need a more specific group model.

## Reading a pooled estimate carefully

An estimated deviation near zero can have two sources. The speaker's observations may lie close to the population relation, or the observations may provide little information and receive strong shrinkage. The estimate alone cannot distinguish these cases. Its uncertainty and the number of observations are part of the interpretation.

::: {.callout-note title="Check the pooling"}
Why should a speaker mean based on two tokens usually receive more shrinkage than a speaker mean based on two hundred consistent tokens? Which quantities in $w_j$ express this difference?
:::

The [next page](random-intercepts.qmd) places one partially pooled baseline deviation in a regression equation.
